section_summary: This section (pages 664–732) contains State Department despatches, telegrams, internal memoranda, Military Intelligence Division reports, and FBI investigative surveys regarding Japanese political, economic, and foreign affairs between late 1940 and early 1941 (with retrospective memoranda into 1942). Key topics include the organizational structure and constitutional debates surrounding Prince Fumimaro Konoe's New Structure and the Imperial Rule Assistance Association (IRAA), along with growing Diet, business, and public criticism of wartime economic controls and food rationing. The documents also examine deteriorating Japanese-American relations following Japan's adherence to the Tripartite Pact, unofficial peace missions and emissary proposals involving Count Yoriyasu Arima and Gracie Hall Roosevelt, rumors of an anti-war military coup d'état led by General Ugaki, and urgent recommendations for the evacuation of American citizens and missionaries from Japan.

subfiles.about: Cross-reference file sheet noting Tokyo Telegram No. 1348 regarding the substance of the Japanese Foreign Minister's address at the America-Japan Society.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Telegram No. 1348 (December 19, 1940): Matsuoka's address to the America-Japan Society luncheon (711.94/1884).
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Address of Foreign Minister at Luncheon of America-Japan Society

subfiles.about: Telegram summarizing Japanese press accounts of War Minister Tojo's meeting with army elders and allegations of Anglo-American interference in Southeast Asia.
subfiles.summary: Press summary: Tojo convened thirteen senior army leaders to appeal for unity; Domei alleges US-backed British economic approach to Indochina; Kokumin cites Hull's talk with the Thai Minister.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 73: Summary Today's Press

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting a confidential conversation between an Embassy officer and Mr. Fujii, personal adviser to Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma.
subfiles.summary: Hiranuma's adviser Fujii says Japan will pursue East Asian leadership at all costs, but neither he nor Hiranuma has abandoned hope of better US relations; he asks to meet Dooman.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 123: Conversation with Baron Hiranuma's Adviser Fujii

subfiles.about: Telegram from Secretary of State Hull suggesting that further conversations with Baron Hiranuma's adviser Fujii might be productive.
subfiles.summary: Hull suggests Grew may pursue conversation with Hiranuma's adviser Fujii if appropriate, referring to Telegram No. 123.
subfiles.title: State Department Telegram No. 217 to Tokyo Regarding Conversations with Fujii

subfiles.about: Confidential State Department digest summarizing Tokyo Telegram No. 123 regarding statements by Baron Hiranuma's adviser Fujii.
subfiles.summary: Confidential digest of Telegram No. 123: Fujii says Japan will go to the limit for East Asian predominance, but he and Hiranuma still hope to improve US relations.
subfiles.title: Digest - Telegram Received: Tokyo No. 123

subfiles.about: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 5268 on an editorial from the Japan News-Week.
subfiles.summary: Fales summarizes Despatch No. 5268, a Japan News-Week 'The Year 1940' editorial: New Structure ended liberalism, Nazi-Fascist embrace cost American and British friendship, and Japan recklessly challenges the US.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 5268

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting and analyzing an editorial from the Japan News-Week reviewing Japan's totalitarian reorganization and international perils in 1940.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits Despatch No. 5268 enclosing an extensive editorial entitled 'The Year 1940' from the December 28, 1940 issue of the Japan News-Week. Grew analyzes the editorial's critique of Japan's departure from traditional constitutional moorings into sweeping political, economic, and social totalitarianism. The enclosed text emphasizes the elimination of political parties and liberalism, severe regimentation of social and religious life, and the heavy unsolved burdens of the China Incident. The editorial strongly deplores the breakdown in Japanese-American relations following the Tripartite Pact, warning that Japanese leaders are gambling on a catastrophic conflict with the United States.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 5268: Transmitting Japanese Press Comment: Editorial Entitled 'The Year 1940' from the Japan News Week of December 28, 1940

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting severe parliamentary criticism of the New Economic Structure and IRAA by Mr. Akaike and Prime Minister Konoe's reply.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports Peers member Akaike attacked the New Economic Structure and IRAA; Konoe replied that wartime demanded control, denied it was Communistic, and called the IRAA a government-people link.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 134: Parliamentary Criticism of the New Structure and IRAA

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum evaluating unofficial Japanese peace overtures involving M. Kleiman, Count Arima, and the John Doe associates.
subfiles.summary: Ballantine finds seized records relate to 1941: Kleiman counted on Count Arima, and John Doe associate Wikawa was Arima's henchman; both approaches came from one Japanese faction.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum Regarding M. Kleiman and John Doe Peace Approaches

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum reporting an impending Washington luncheon meeting concerning M. Kleiman's unofficial U.S.-Japan peace proposal.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton notes a planned Washington luncheon with Kleiman and Japanese representatives to lobby Roosevelt to send an unofficial emissary; the Department judged the scheme improper.
subfiles.title: Department of State Memorandum on M. Kleiman's Peace Proposal and Unofficial Emissary Project

subfiles.about: Memorandum examining file records of a proposed 1940–1941 mission by Gracie Hall Roosevelt to negotiate a settlement in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ballantine reviews records of a 1940-41 plan for Gracie Hall Roosevelt to negotiate in Japan for a $50,000 fee and seven-point program; it collapsed when Nisiyama disavowed the program.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Proposed Mission of Gracie Hall Roosevelt to Japan

subfiles.about: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 5315 regarding the organization of the IRAA.
subfiles.summary: Fales on Despatch No. 5315: the IRAA's structure, with the Prime Minister as President, advisory bodies, five bureaus and cooperative councils; an ordinance of December 26, 1940 placed it under Cabinet jurisdiction.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 5315

subfiles.about: Extensive despatch transmitting detailed reporting, translated regulations, and structural diagrams of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew provides a comprehensive study of the origin, political character, and administrative machinery of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association (Taisei Yokusankai). Grew traces the movement from Premier Fumimaro Konoe's August 1940 declarations through Count Yoriyasu Arima's Preparatory Commission, the inaugural gathering of October 12, 1940, and ongoing debates over constitutionality and relations with the Diet. Enclosure No. 1 provides a complete English translation of the seventeen articles of the Regulations of the Imperial Rule Assisting Movement. Enclosure No. 2 consists of detailed structural charts illustrating the hierarchy from the President and Advisory Body down through the Secretariat bureaus (General Affairs, Systematization, Policy, Planning, Diet) and the national and prefectural cooperative council networks.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 5315: The Organization of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association

subfiles.about: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 5303 on the Bungei Shunju public opinion poll.
subfiles.summary: Fales on Despatch No. 5303: Bungei Shunju poll of 685 respondents; 600 said the public did not understand the New Structure, and 412 thought US-Japan war avoidable, 262 not.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 5303

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting and analyzing a ten-question public opinion survey from Bungei Shunju magazine regarding Japanese political, economic, and war attitudes.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports on a public opinion poll conducted among 685 readers of the monthly magazine Bungei Shunju, representing government workers, professionals, and white-collar employees. Grew provides a detailed breakdown of responses to ten questions covering the New Structure, economic reform, war with the United States, youth ambition, stock speculation, radio programming, political leadership, careers in China, neighborhood leagues, and household income. The findings reveal widespread popular confusion and lack of enthusiasm regarding the New Structure, powerful sentiment for economic renovation (especially among Osaka merchants and farmers), dissatisfaction with aging political leaders, and a notable majority hoping that war with the United States can be averted.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 5303: Poll of Public Opinion by the Bungei Shunju Magazine

subfiles.about: Letter from FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover transmitting an intelligence report on Japanese conditions to Assistant Secretary of State Berle.
subfiles.summary: J. Edgar Hoover sends Berle an FBI St. Paul report on economic, military and political information from an American metallurgist back from Japan.
subfiles.title: FBI Letter Transmitting Japanese Intelligence Survey to Assistant Secretary Berle

subfiles.about: FBI intelligence report based on debriefings of metallurgical expert Louis H. Berry regarding Japanese steel, truck manufacturing, scrap shortages, and naval views.
subfiles.summary: FBI report on Louis H. Berry, back from eighteen months in Japan: steel hurt by scrap embargo, sixty days of gasoline, and Axis alliance forced by the Army.
subfiles.title: FBI Report: General Japanese Intelligence Survey (Interview with Louis H. Berry)

subfiles.about: Confidential telegram reporting unverified intelligence of a planned military coup d'état led by General Ugaki to avert war with the United States.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports an unverified rumor of a coup modeled on February 26 to topple Konoe and avert war with the US, with Ugaki leading, Masaki as War Minister and Ikeda for Finance.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 276: Reported Impending Military Coup d'État

subfiles.about: State Department paraphrase of Tokyo Telegram No. 276 regarding rumors of an anti-war military coup d'état in Japan.
subfiles.summary: State Department paraphrase of Telegram No. 276 on the rumored Army coup, prepared for naval and military intelligence.
subfiles.title: State Department Paraphrase of Tokyo Telegram No. 276
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence and Military Intelligence Division

subfiles.about: Telegram from Dr. Ralph E. Diffendorfer requesting an urgent meeting with State Department Far Eastern officials following his return from Japan and Korea.
subfiles.summary: Methodist missions secretary Diffendorfer wires that he returned from Japan and Korea, where Grew urged him to confer with the Department.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Ralph E. Diffendorfer Requesting State Department Conference
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck and Maxwell M. Hamilton

subfiles.about: Memorandum of conversation with Dr. Ralph E. Diffendorfer on totalitarian trends in Japan, German influence, Matsuoka's attitude, and missionary withdrawal.
subfiles.summary: Joseph W. Ballantine records a comprehensive conference between Dr. Ralph E. Diffendorfer of the Methodist Board of Foreign Missions and State Department officials Stanley K. Hornbeck, Maxwell M. Hamilton, and Ballantine. Diffendorfer recounts his impressions from visiting Japan and Korea, observing strong extremist control, pervasive totalitarian and youth mobilization, and growing German presence and influence. He describes a tense interview with Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka, who warned the United States to stay on its side of the Pacific and declared Japan would never abandon China. Diffendorfer strongly advocates the immediate withdrawal of American missionaries and citizens from Japan, praising Consul General Marsh in Keijo for efficient evacuation handling and noting the persistent activities of German Jesuit priest Father Bitter in Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Department of State Memorandum of Conversation: Dr. Diffendorfer's Impressions in Japan and Views on Evacuation

subfiles.about: Telegram summarizing Japanese press criticism of the Diet recess, IRAA shortcomings, Cabinet weakness, and Prince Konoe's leadership.
subfiles.summary: Grew summarizes press criticism during the Diet recess: Diet opposition to the New Structure, failure to settle the China Incident, Konoe's weak leadership and illness, and calls for cabinet reorganization.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 376: Press Criticism of Diet, Government, and Konoe Cabinet

subfiles.about: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing Military Intelligence Division Report No. 10,257 on Japanese internal and foreign affairs.
subfiles.summary: Fales summarizes MID Report 10,257: Hiranuma's appointment, business opposition to the Planning Board, election law reform, Nomura's reluctant Washington post, Matsuoka's statements and press condemnation of the US China loan.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on MID Report No. 10,257

subfiles.about: Extensive Military Attaché report analyzing Japanese domestic politics, military statements, Hiranuma's entry into the Cabinet, economic struggles, election reforms, rationing, Nomura's appointment, and Matsuoka's foreign policy.
subfiles.summary: The U.S. Military Attaché in Tokyo submits Report No. 10,257 (Comments on Current Events - No. 39) evaluating critical domestic and international developments in Japan. The report reviews a joint Army-Navy declaration pledging total support for the New Structure and IRAA while urging national production expansion and suppression of impure political movements. It details Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma's appointment as Minister Without Portfolio alongside Naoki Hoshino, followed by a major political conflict between the Cabinet Planning Board and leading financiers under Baron Seinosuke Go over a drastic, allegedly confiscatory economic plan. The report also examines controversial election law amendments establishing voter councils and family-head voting criteria that threatened to disenfranchise prominent figures such as Minister Ishiguro and General Oshima. Finally, it surveys the widening rationing of food and consumer commodities, Admiral Kichisaburo Nomura's appointment as Ambassador to Washington, and Foreign Minister Matsuoka's press conference disclaiming territorial ambitions in the Dutch East Indies while reaffirming core alignment with the Axis.
subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division Report No. 10,257: Comments on Current Events - No. 39
